passages.title: Calcium Homeostasis
passages.body_text:
Calcium ions are needed not only for bone mineralization but for tooth health, regulation of the heart rate and strength of contraction, blood coagulation, contraction of smooth and skeletal muscle cells, and regulation of nerve impulse conduction.
The normal level of calcium in the blood is about 10 mg/dL. When the body cannot maintain this level, a person will experience hypocalcaemia, a condition characterized by abnormally low levels of calcium, or hypercalcaemia, a condition characterized by abnormally high levels of calcium. So, calcium homeostasis is critical.
The skeletal, endocrine, and digestive systems play a role in this, and also kidneys do. These body systems work together to maintain a normal calcium level in the blood as shown in the figure.
The only way calcium can enter the body is through the diet or by injection. The bones act as a storage site for calcium, and the body deposits calcium in the bones when blood levels get too high and it releases calcium when blood levels drop too low. This process is regulated by parathyroid hormone (PTH), vitamin D, and calcitonin.
Cells of the parathyroid gland have plasma membrane receptors for calcium. When the receptors are full, the parathyroid gland stops secreting PTH. When calcium is not binding to these receptors, the cells release PTH, which stimulates osteoclast proliferation and resorption of bone by osteoclasts. This demineralization process releases calcium into the blood. PTH promotes reabsorption of calcium from the urine by the kidneys, so that the calcium returns to the blood. Finally, PTH stimulates the synthesis of vitamin D, which in turn, stimulates calcium absorption from any digested food in the small intestine. When all these processes return blood calcium levels to normal, there is enough calcium to bind with the receptors on the surface of the cells of the parathyroid glands, and this cycle of events is turned off.
The thyroid gland (which secretes both thyroxin hormone and calcitonin hormone), when blood levels of calcium get too high, is stimulated to release calcitonin, which inhibits osteoclast activity and stimulates calcium uptake by the bones, and also decreases reabsorption of calcium by the kidneys, and all these actions lower blood levels of calcium. When blood calcium levels return to normal, the thyroid gland stops secreting calcitonin.
Vitamin D is required for calcium absorption by the gut and acts as a hormone in its activated form, stimulating absorption of calcium by the small intestine. Low vitamin D could lead to insufficient levels of calcium in the blood so the calcium is being released from the bones by the action of PTH. The reduction of calcium from the bones can make them weak and subject to fracture.

passages.title: Crossing Over in Maize (Creighton & McClintock)
passages.body_text:
Thomas Hunt Morgan proposed that segments of paternal and maternal chromatids cross over (break and re-anneal) during meiosis I. If Morgan was correct, it meant that chromosomes exchange genetic information when they cross over. Was Morgan's hypothesis valid? Did crossing over imply a breaking and reattachment of chromosome segments?
An experiment that Harriet Creighton and Barbara McClintock performed in 1931 on Zea mays (maize or corn) helped to answer these questions. These researchers worked with strains of maize that differed in two ways. In one strain, chromosome 9 was longer than usual and had a knob at one end. In the other strain, chromosome 9 was of normal length and lacked this knob. The knobby, long chromosome 9 consisted of genes that led to the production of colored, waxy kernels. The shorter, knobless chromosome 9 had genes that encoded instructions for colorless, starchy kernels.
Note that Morgan's hypothesis predicts that if crossing over between the two genes occurs, the resulting gametes should have a new type of chromosome 9: short with a knob, or long with no knob. The offspring that have these chromosomes should also have a unique combination of traits: kernels that are colored and starchy, or kernels that are colorless and waxy.
Creighton and McClintock tested these predictions by arranging matings between individuals from each strain. Their offspring had one copy of the long, knobbed chromosome 9 and one copy of the short, knobless chromosome 9. When Creighton and McClintock compared the chromosomes observed in offspring with the morphology of their kernels, the results conformed exactly to the predictions.
Every individual with two copies of the short, knobless chromosome 9 had colorless, starchy kernels. Every individual with two copies of the long, knobbed chromosome 9 had colored, waxy kernels. Based on these results, Morgan's hypothesis became widely accepted. A physical exchange of maternal and paternal chromatids occurs during crossing over, resulting in chromosomes with a combination of genetic information from the mother and father.

passages.title: Human Cloning?
passages.body_text:
Biologists can harvest nuclei from the somatic cells of mice, cows and sheep and use them to produce embryos. These nuclear transfer experiments produce offspring that are genetically identical to the individual providing the donor nucleus. A group of genetically identical organisms is called a clone, so the process of creating individuals by transferring nuclei into enucleated eggs is called cloning. Can humans be cloned?
Why would anyone want to clone a human? Proponents of the technology contend that cloning by nuclear transfer would allow otherwise infertile couples to have offspring that are genetically related — in fact, identical — to one of the parents. Another argument is that cloning would allow a family to replace a dying child. Opponents of the technology are concerned that, in an attempt at immortality, a dictator or wealthy eccentric could finance clones of themselves in perpetuity.
Even benign uses of human cloning create ethical dilemmas that are yet to be thoroughly debated or resolved. What is the effect on a family of having children that are genetically identical to a parent? Would the child be less likely to respect and obey that parent? Would the child suffer from the expectation that it should turn out exactly like that parent? Given the number and seriousness of the questions involved, several nations have proposed a prohibition on all research related to cloning humans.
In addition to the legal and ethical issues involved, there are significant technical hurdles to overcome before human cloning is feasible. Of the species that have been successfully cloned, monkeys and mice are most closely related to humans. Less than three percent of nuclear transfers result in viable mice, however. Most result in aborted pregnancies; some produce individuals that die soon after birth. Currently, the success rate is similar in cloning sheep and cows, and production of deformed newborns has occurred. Most people regard a failure rate this high as unacceptable for humans.

passages.title: Carbon Dioxide Transport in the Blood
passages.body_text:
The blood carries carbon dioxide partly as undissociated carbon dioxide in solution in the plasma, partly as hydrogencarbonate ions in solution in the plasma, and partly combined with haemoglobin in the red blood cells. Carbon dioxide is continually produced by respiring cells. It diffuses from the cells into blood plasma, from where some of it diffuses into the red blood cells. In the cytoplasm of red blood cells there is an enzyme, carbonic anhydrase, which catalyzes the reaction: CO2 + H2O <-> H2CO3 <-> H+ + HCO3-.
Most of the hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO3-) produced during this reaction then diffuse out of the red blood cell into the blood plasma, where they are carried in solution. About 85% of the carbon dioxide is transported by the blood in this way.
Some carbon dioxide, however, does not dissociate, but remains as carbon dioxide molecules. Some of these simply dissolve in the blood plasma; about 5% of the total is carried in this form. Others diffuse into the red blood cells, but instead of undergoing the reaction catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase, combine directly with the terminal amine groups (-NH2) of some haemoglobin molecules, forming carbamino-haemoglobin. About 10% of the carbon dioxide is carried in this way.
When blood reaches the lungs, the reactions described above go into reverse. The relatively low concentration of carbon dioxide in the alveoli compared with that in the blood causes carbon dioxide to diffuse from the blood into the air in the alveoli, stimulating carbon dioxide to leave carbamino-haemoglobin, while hydrogencarbonate and hydrogen ions recombine to form carbon dioxide molecules once more. This leaves the haemoglobin molecules free to combine with oxygen, ready to begin another circuit of the body.

passages.title: Volcanoes and Magma
passages.body_text:
The distribution of volcanoes on Earth's surface is not random. Only about 5 percent of magma erupts far from plate boundaries. The volcanoes associated with convergent plate boundaries are characterized by explosive eruptions and form two major belts. The larger belt is called the Ring of Fire, stretching along the western coasts of North and South America, across the Aleutian Islands, and down the eastern coast of Asia. The smaller belt's general outline corresponds to the boundaries between the Eurasian, African, and Arabian plates. Divergent volcanism at ocean ridges tends to be non-explosive, with effusions of large amounts of lava.
About two thirds of Earth's volcanism occurs underwater along divergent boundaries at ocean ridges. Some volcanoes form far from plate boundaries over hot spots, for example, the Hawaiian Islands, located over a plume of magma. The magma chamber acts as a source for magma injections (dykes, sheets, sills) into the surrounding crust and to the surface of the associated volcano.
The activity of a volcano depends on the composition of the magma. Most rocks begin to melt at temperatures between 800°C and 1200°C. In addition to temperature, pressure and the presence of water also affect the formation of magma. As pressure increases, the temperature at which a substance melts also increases. Temperature and silica content affect the viscosity of magma. In general, cooler magma has a higher viscosity and tends to resist flowing. Magma with high silica content tends to be thick and sticky, and because it is thick, it tends to trap gases, which produces explosive eruptions.

passages.title: The Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-T) Extinction
passages.body_text:
70 million years ago, dinosaurs walked, crawled, swam and flew all over the earth. But sometime between 65 and 66 million years ago, all non-flying (non-avian) dinosaurs suddenly went extinct. This was called the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction (also called the Cretaceous-Tertiary or K-T extinction), and it didn't just kill the dinosaurs: about 80% of life on the planet was wiped out.
For years, paleontologists didn't really know what could have caused such an apocalyptic extinction, but today scientific consensus has settled on the asteroid impact theory. According to this theory, the extinction was triggered when a huge asteroid struck the earth around 66 million years ago near the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico. The crater created by that impact is still there today — it's called the Chicxulub crater. Today, the Chicxulub crater is about 180 kilometers across and 2 kilometers deep, and scientists estimate the asteroid itself would have been around 10 kilometers across.
The force of this enormous asteroid caused a wave of tsunamis, earthquakes, and landslides all over the world. The collision sent 10,000 billion tons of carbon dioxide spewing into the atmosphere, causing instant and dramatic climate change. Scientists estimate that the debris from the explosion, plus the smoke from subsequent fires, created enough particulate matter to temporarily destroy the ozone layer. The clouds of dust blocked the sun, changing the climate of the entire planet and causing a sudden drop in global temperature. Plants couldn't survive without enough sunlight, meaning death for plant-eating dinosaurs, which in turn ended the carnivorous dinosaurs that preyed on them.
Scientists have also found evidence for the asteroid impact theory in rocks from the Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary. These rocks have: (1) high levels of iridium, a mineral rare on Earth but common in asteroids; (2) a lot of ejecta, including tektites — small pieces of glass produced by the heat and pressure of rock collisions; and (3) a lot of quartz with fractured crystals, which can be fractured by a massive shock.

passages.title: The Mediterranean Salinity Crisis
passages.body_text:
In 1970, an undersea drilling project began taking samples of the Mediterranean's ocean floor. They discovered an area of salt up to 3 kilometers thick and located 100-200 meters below the ocean floor, which they named the M-reflector. By studying the salt, they found that the Mediterranean Sea must have dried up at one point millions of years ago for an extensive period.
They called this drying of the sea the Mediterranean Salinity Crisis (MSC). The MSC began approximately 6 million years ago (MYA) and lasted until around 5.3 MYA (Late Miocene time) — a span of well over half a million years. Although scientists are still not completely sure about the cause of the MSC, there is strong evidence that sea level had dropped about 70 meters prior to the Crisis, likely due to global cooling allowing water to freeze into glaciers and icebergs, lowering the ocean's sea level.
This drop in sea level made it difficult for the Atlantic Ocean to flow into the Mediterranean, which began receiving much less water. The Mediterranean evaporates at a very fast pace because it is located in a dry area. Meanwhile, the ocean floor beneath where the Atlantic connected to the Mediterranean began to rise, as Southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa moved towards each other, eventually rising high enough to form land that completely separated the Mediterranean from the Atlantic.
As the water in the Mediterranean evaporated, the salt left behind built up in layers on the floor. Two major salts deposited were Halite and Gypsum, with some deposit areas 800 meters deep. However, the salt did not deposit as quickly as the water evaporated, so the remaining water became very salty, becoming deadly to all marine life.

passages.title: Geophysics and Seismic Exploration
passages.body_text:
Geophysics is the non-invasive investigation of subsurface conditions through measuring, analyzing, and interpreting physical fields at the surface. It employs physical methods at, above, or below (via borehole) the earth's surface to measure physical properties of the subsurface — dielectric, susceptibility, density, wave velocity, resistivity, elastic, permittivity — and their anomalies.
Seismic waves, the same tool used to study earthquakes, are frequently used to search for oil and natural gas deep below Earth's surface. Seismic waves are sent deep into the Earth and allowed to bounce back; geophysicists record the waves to learn about reservoirs beneath the surface.
Reflection seismology is commonly used during onshore exploration: seismic waves are sent underground, and when they bounce back they're picked up by surface sensors, providing information on the geophysical properties of a potential oil reserve. The most common onshore method is vibroseis — large, heavy vehicles that apply a base plate to the Earth with a hydraulic system that vibrates the plate over a predetermined frequency range.
In offshore exploration, seismic airguns release a chamber of compressed air into the water, creating a pressure wave that penetrates the seabed, illuminates geological structures, and reflects information back through the water, where it's detected by hydrophone cables.

passages.title: What Defines a Human Being?
passages.body_text:
From a biological point of view, what is a human being? Historically, scientists and philosophers have argued that humans have one or more unique characteristics that set us apart from other organisms. For decades this defining characteristic was thought to be tool use. But then Jane Goodall, who pioneered the study of common chimpanzees in the field, observed that chimps collect and modify twigs to "fish" for termites or ants and eat them.
Tool-use is a culturally transmitted behavior in chimpanzees, meaning it is learned — in this case, a mother teaching her offspring. Later, Goodall and other biologists reported additional examples of tool use by common chimps, pygmy chimps, baboons, sea otters, and a wide variety of birds.
In response, some observers argued that the defining characteristic of humans was not toolmaking but the use of language based on the abstract symbols we call words and letters. But researchers have now been able to teach chimps rudimentary aspects of American Sign Language. This sends an important message: the ability to learn and use abstract symbols and grammatical rules is not unique to humans.
In short, there may be no single characteristic that "defines" humans. Instead, most contemporary biologists characterize our species by a suite of traits that are not necessarily unique. Humans are an intensely social, bipedal animal with a brain that is absolutely huge given our body size. Humans also have a particularly long period of sexual immaturity, or childhood, accompanied by extraordinarily high levels of parental care. Finally, most biologists emphasize that the changes in human morphology and behavior over the past 40,000 years have probably been dominated by cultural evolution — changes fashioned by teaching and learning — rather than evolution by natural selection.
Recently, molecular genetics has furnished a new perspective on this question. When Svante Pääbo and co-workers sequenced a 10,156-base-pair segment from the X chromosomes of humans and common chimpanzees, they found the sequences were identical at almost 99 percent of the 10,156 sites. This raises the question: which 1% to 2% of the human genome is responsible for the morphological and behavioral differences between chimps and humans? Will it be possible to identify the alleles responsible for our bipedal posture, large brains, slow rate of sexual maturation, and huge capacity for learning? Researchers have only begun to tackle these questions, but with a variety of genome analysis projects now under way, answers may soon be forthcoming.

passages.title: HNPCC and Mismatch Repair Genes
passages.body_text:
Cancer geneticists have known for decades that families can have predispositions to certain types of cancers, including breast cancer and some skin cancers. A common type of colon cancer called hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) also runs in families. Affected individuals frequently develop tumors of the colon, ovary, and other organs before age 50. A major breakthrough in understanding HNPCC occurred in the early 1990s, when a gene associated with susceptibility to HNPCC was mapped to a specific region of chromosome 2.
Meanwhile, a different group of investigators was trying to determine if humans have mismatch repair genes similar to those found in E. coli. This work accelerated once the DNA sequence of the mutS gene was determined, and a mismatch repair gene identified in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae turned out to be extremely similar to mutS — so similar that the bacterial and yeast genes were considered homologous, tracing their ancestry to a gene in a common ancestor.
Using sequence information from these homologous genes, researchers located a similar sequence in the human genome, called hMSH (human mutS homolog). Then it was discovered that the hMSH gene mapped to the same region of chromosome 2 as the HNPCC susceptibility gene.
The link between a defect in mismatch repair and HNPCC was cemented when it was confirmed that individuals suffering from this cancer have mutated forms of hMSH. Cells from these patients had mutation rates 100 times that of normal cells when grown in culture, and follow-up studies confirmed that this increased mutation rate is indeed due to defective mismatch repair.
Although the early E. coli experiments seemed to be basic research without practical application, because humans, yeast, and bacteria share a common evolutionary history, and because DNA synthesis and repair are fundamental to all cells, those experiments made a major advance in cancer biology possible. If individuals with mutant forms of hMSH can be identified early in life, dietary changes and therapy could significantly reduce their risk of developing cancer.

passages.title: HIV, Reverse Transcriptase, and AZT Resistance
passages.body_text:
Once a virus has entered a cell, it cannot begin making copies of itself immediately. Only a subset of viruses contains all the enzymes necessary for transcribing their own genome, and none can make the ribosomes and tRNAs necessary for translating mRNAs. For a particle to make more particles, it must exploit the host cell's biosynthetic machinery.
HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is a retrovirus. Two copies of the RNA genome and about 50 molecules of reverse transcriptase lie inside the core of each particle. Soon after these molecules enter a host cell, reverse transcriptase makes cDNA versions of the viral genome using nucleotides and ATP from the cell. A viral protein called integrase then catalyzes the cutting of host DNA, insertion of the viral genome into the host DNA sequence, and reannealing of the DNA strand — integrating a copy of the HIV genome into the host chromosome.
When researchers first searched for a drug to stop HIV infections, they focused on disrupting this part of the infection cycle, aiming to obstruct reverse transcriptase. The first widely prescribed anti-AIDS drug, azidothymidine (AZT), is so similar in structure to the nucleotide thymidine that reverse transcriptase sometimes incorporates AZT instead of thymidine into a growing DNA strand. This terminates synthesis because AZT will not accept the addition of another deoxyribonucleotide, blocking viral replication.
AZT was extremely effective in the laboratory and slowed infection dramatically in early trials. But not long after widespread use, most patients stopped responding. Researchers isolating HIV strains from non-responding patients found these strains resistant to AZT in culture. Sequencing revealed an identical series of mutations in the part of the reverse transcriptase enzyme that binds thymidine — mutations correlated with resistance, making the enzyme less likely to be fooled by the drug, so mutant strains could complete replication even with AZT present.
This sequence of events parallels how natural selection has favored rifampin-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, now responsible for a resurgence of tuberculosis in the industrial world.

passages.title: Calcium Regulation by PTH and Calcitonin
passages.body_text:
Regulation of blood calcium concentration is important for generating muscle contractions and nerve impulses, which are electrically stimulated. If calcium levels get too high, membrane permeability to sodium decreases and membranes become less responsive. If calcium levels get too low, membrane permeability to sodium increases and convulsions or muscle spasms may result.
Blood calcium levels are regulated by parathyroid hormone (PTH), produced by the parathyroid glands and released in response to low blood calcium. PTH increases calcium levels by targeting the skeleton, kidneys, and intestine. In the skeleton, PTH stimulates osteoclasts (which reabsorb bone, releasing calcium into the blood) and inhibits osteoblasts (which deposit bone, reducing calcium deposition). In the kidneys, PTH directly stimulates calcium re-absorption. In the intestine, its effect is indirect: PTH triggers formation of calcitriol (active vitamin D), which acts on the intestine to increase dietary calcium absorption. PTH release is inhibited by rising blood calcium.
Hyperparathyroidism (overproduction of PTH) leads to excessive calcium removal from bones into the blood, producing structural bone weakness/fractures plus nervous system impairment from high blood calcium. Hypoparathyroidism (underproduction of PTH) causes extremely low blood calcium, impairing muscle function and potentially causing tetany (severe sustained muscle contraction).
Calcitonin, produced by the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid, has the opposite effect to PTH: it decreases blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts, stimulating osteoblasts, and stimulating calcium excretion by the kidneys, adding calcium to bones to promote structural integrity. Calcitonin is most important in children (stimulating bone growth), during pregnancy (reducing maternal bone loss), and during prolonged starvation (reducing bone mass loss). In healthy, non-pregnant, unstarved adults, its role is unclear.

passages.title: Mineral Properties: Lustre, Hardness, Colour, Streak
passages.body_text:
Earth's crust is composed of about 3000 minerals. Minerals play important roles in forming rocks and in shaping Earth's surface. A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a specific chemical composition and a definite crystalline structure, often exhibited by the crystal shape itself.
Lustre: the way a mineral reflects light from its surface. There are two types — metallic and non-metallic. Minerals with non-metallic lustres, such as calcite, gypsum, sulfur, and quartz, do not shine like metals; non-metallic lustres might be described as dull, pearly, waxy, silky, or earthy.
Hardness: one of the most useful and reliable tests for identifying minerals. Hardness measures how easily a mineral can be scratched. German geologist Friedrich Mohs developed a scale comparing an unknown mineral's hardness to ten known minerals. These were selected because they are easily recognized and, except for diamond, readily found in nature.
Colour: one of the most noticeable characteristics of a mineral, sometimes caused by trace elements or compounds. Quartz, for example, occurs in a variety of colours — red jasper, purple amethyst, and orange citrine contain different amounts and forms of iron, while rose quartz contains manganese or titanium. Milky quartz's appearance is caused by trapped bubbles of gas and liquid. In general, colour is one of the least reliable clues to a mineral's identity.
Streak: the colour of a mineral when broken up and powdered. The streak of a non-metallic mineral is usually white; streak is most useful for identifying metallic minerals.

passages.title: Seafloor Spreading and Paleomagnetism
passages.body_text:
In the late 1950s, geologist Harry Hess suggested that the valley at the center of mid-ocean ridges was a crack, or rift, in the Earth's crust, where magma from deep inside Earth rises to fill the crack. As the ocean floor moves away from the ridge, rising magma cools and solidifies into new rock that replaces the ocean floor.
This process, named seafloor spreading by geologist Robert Dietz (1952), forms new ocean lithosphere as magma rises and solidifies at a mid-ocean ridge. Hess suggested that if the ocean floor is moving, the continents might be moving too — that seafloor spreading was the mechanism Wegener had failed to find.
Still, Hess's ideas were only hypotheses. More evidence came in the mid-1960s through paleomagnetism, the study of the magnetic properties of rocks. Scientists noticed that the striped magnetic pattern on one side of a mid-ocean ridge is a mirror image of the pattern on the other side. These patterns show alternating bands of normal and reversed polarity matching the geomagnetic reversal time scale, suggesting that as new seafloor forms at a mid-ocean ridge, it records reversals in Earth's magnetic field.

passages.title: The Mesozoic Era and Mass Extinction
passages.body_text:
Earth's surface is constantly changing: mountains form and erode; oceans rise and recede. As conditions change, some organisms flourish and later become extinct. Evidence of these changes is recorded in rock layers, and scientists have developed a geologic time scale describing the sequence and length of these changes.
The geologic era that began about 251 million years ago and ended about 65 million years ago is the Mesozoic Era, divided into three periods (Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous). Dinosaurs became the dominant life form during the Jurassic period, and the fossil record indicates two major groups of dinosaurs evolved.
Paleontologist Paul Sereno (1995), working in a previously unexplored region of Morocco, discovered an enormous dinosaur skull nearly 1.6 m long. Given the skull size, Sereno concluded the animal's skeleton must have been about 14 m long — roughly the length of a full-sized school bus — even larger than Tyrannosaurus rex. The dinosaur, dated to about 95 million years old, most likely chased prey on large, powerful hind legs, and its bladelike teeth meant certain death for its prey.
The Mesozoic Era ended with one of the most extensive mass extinctions. Group I of scientists thinks this extinction was caused by environmental changes resulting from continental movement and increased volcanic activity. Group II thinks an asteroid crashed into Earth, raising enough dust to block the Sun's rays for years; as Earth's climate cooled, plant life died and many animal species went extinct.

passages.title: The Rock Cycle
passages.body_text:
Scientists think Earth began as a melted mixture of many different materials. These materials underwent a physical change as they cooled and solidified, becoming the first igneous rocks. Igneous rock continues to form today: liquid rock changes to a solid when lava brought to Earth's surface by volcanoes hardens, or far more slowly when magma deep beneath the surface solidifies. The mineral composition of an igneous rock is determined by the chemical composition of the magma from which it formed; each type of igneous rock has a specific mineral composition.
While new rocks form, old rocks are broken down by other processes. Weathering is the process by which wind, water, and gravity break up rock. During erosion, broken-up rock pieces are carried by water, wind, or ice and deposited as sediments elsewhere, piling up to form sedimentary rock. Sedimentary rock may itself be broken down and become another sedimentary rock. As sediments pile up, plant and animal remains are buried. Tremendous pressure, extreme heat, and chemical processes can also alter the form of existing rock, producing metamorphic rock. Any of the three major rock types can be changed into another, as shown in the rock cycle.

passages.title: Muscular Dystrophy and Gene Therapy
passages.body_text:
Muscular dystrophy (MD) is one of the most common genetic diseases, occurring almost exclusively in boys, who suffer from a degenerative disease. It has been estimated that 28.8% of cases are due to a spontaneous genetic mutation, although it is normally inherited. MD results in progressive degeneration of skeletal and cardiac muscle fiber cells, weakening the muscle and eventually leading to death due to cardiac or respiratory failure. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common form of MD apparent from birth. Some people are instead struck later in life by a related, milder form known as Becker's muscular dystrophy (BMD).
DMD is caused by a mutation in the gene coding for the protein dystrophin, rendering it nonfunctional. BMD, also resulting from a mutation, is usually characterized by a partially functional dystrophin product, accounting for its later onset. Dystrophin is found on the inner surface of the plasma membrane in normal muscle tissue. The gene coding for dystrophin is the longest known gene in the human body, at 2.4 megabases, accounting for 0.1% of the genome.
Gene therapy — therapeutic alteration of the genome as a treatment for genetic disorders — poses formidable challenges, including targeting altered genes to the correct cells. One method of introducing genes into cells is to coat the DNA with an envelope of cationic, amphipathic lipids, forming liposome-DNA complexes. The lipids present their charged surface to the DNA molecules, giving the complex an outer hydrophobic coating that enables it to cross the plasma membrane.

passages.title: Bacterial Plasmid Gene Transfer
passages.body_text:
Many bacteria contain small, circular DNA molecules called plasmids, which can be transferred from one bacterium to another. For this to occur, the plasmid replicates and produces a linear copy of itself; the relative position of genes is the same on the original plasmid and on the linear copy, except the two ends of the linear copy do not immediately connect. While replication occurs, one end of the linear copy leaves the donor bacterium and enters the recipient. Thus, the order in which genes are replicated is the same as the order in which they are transferred. Unless interrupted, the entire plasmid is transferred and its two ends connect in the recipient.
Four researchers studied how six genes — F, X, R, S, A, and G — on a specific plasmid are donated by a type of bacterium. They determined the entire plasmid transfers in 90 minutes at a constant rate, with genes evenly spaced so that one gene transfers every 15 minutes. They disagreed about the order of replication/transfer:
Researcher 1: Replication always begins between Gene F and Gene X; Gene X is replicated first and Gene F last.
Researcher 2: Replication always begins between Gene F and Gene X, but direction varies — whichever of F or X is replicated first, the other is replicated last.
Researcher 3: Replication can begin between any two genes, then proceeds clockwise (with respect to the figure); e.g., if Gene S is first, Gene A is second, and Gene R is last.
Researcher 4: Replication can begin between any two genes, and can proceed in either direction, so the order varies.

passages.title: Coronary Heart Disease Study (2001)
passages.body_text:
In 2001, a study of heart disease included 5,137 adults: 2,292 men and 2,445 women, all aged 49 to 70, none showing signs of coronary artery disease at the start. After 14-16 years of follow-up, it was found that:
I. 151 men and 37 women showed evidence of coronary artery disease that would account for a heart attack.
II. 102 men and 18 women died of coronary artery disease before reaching age 65.
III. 58 percent of men and 39 percent of women died within one hour of having a heart attack.
IV. For both men and women, sudden death was more likely if they were under age 55 at the time of the attack.
V. Not all heart attacks produce symptoms — a considerable number of men and women had a myocardial infarction (heart muscle damage) without knowing it; of those "silent coronaries," 22 percent of men and 35 percent of women did not know muscle damage had occurred.

passages.title: Sheep Blood Type Genetics
passages.body_text:
The 4 blood types in sheep are A, B, AB, and O, determined by alleles each parent contributes. There are three possible alleles: type-A (I^A), type-B (I^B), and type-O (I^O). Both I^A and I^B are dominant to I^O. An individual with one I^A and one I^O has type-A blood; one I^B and one I^O has type-B blood. An individual with one I^A and one I^B has type-AB blood, due to codominance.
Analysis 1: 1,000 type-O males mated with 1,000 type-AB females. Offspring observed: Type A 50%, Type B 50%.
Analysis 2: 200 type-A offspring from Analysis 1 mated with 200 type-O mates (unrelated). Offspring observed: Type A 50%, Type O 50%.
Analysis 3: 100 type-A offspring from Analysis 1 mated with 100 type-B offspring from Analysis 1. Offspring observed: Type A 25%, Type B 25%, Type AB 25%, Type O 25%.

passages.title: Stickleback Fish Courtship and Territorial Behavior
passages.body_text:
The complex behavior of the three-spined male stickleback fish has been studied extensively as a model of species behavior in courtship and mating. After a male migrates to a suitable spot, he builds a spawning nest of sand and sediment. When courting, he performs a special "zigzag" dance; the female then follows the male to the nest, where she spawns and he fertilizes the eggs. Male sticklebacks also exhibit territorial behaviors, such as defending nesting or feeding sites from other fish. A biologist performed three experiments to learn more about stickleback behavior.
Experiment 1: Tank 1 and Tank 2 are set up identically, one male stickleback in each; both build nests. The male from Tank 1 is removed and replaced with an egg-laden female; the male from Tank 2 is removed and introduced into Tank 1. In Tank 1, the new male does not perform the zigzag dance, no spawning occurs, and the male retreats to a corner of the tank.
Experiment 2: A male stickleback builds a nest. A fat, round male is introduced. The original male performs the zigzag dance and attempts to lead the round male to the nest; the round male refuses, flapping his fins and swimming in circles. The first male then flaps his fins, circles his nest, and occasionally prods the other fish to a far corner of the tank.
Experiment 3: A small, flat-shaped female is introduced into a tank where a male has built a nest. The male circles the female a few times, then retreats to a corner of the tank.

passages.title: Radiometric Dating
passages.body_text:
Radiometric dating is the process of determining the age of rocks from the decay of radioactive elements. Geologists use radiometric dating to estimate how long ago rocks formed and to infer the ages of fossils contained within those rocks. Radioactive atoms are inherently unstable; over time, radioactive "parent atoms X" decay into stable "daughter atoms Y." When molten rock cools, forming igneous rocks, radioactive atoms are trapped inside and afterward decay at a predictable rate. By measuring the quantity of unstable atoms left in a rock and comparing it to the quantity of stable daughter atoms, scientists can estimate the time elapsed since the rock formed.
(Reference figures: Fig. 1 — cross section of an area with dikes and schist; Fig. 2 — isotope decay curve; Fig. 3 — geologic time scale.)

passages.title: Wind Deflation and Soil Erosion Experiments
passages.body_text:
During deflation, small particles of sediment or soil are moved by the wind. Clay, silt, and fine sand are often moved this way. Deflation sometimes occurs because plant life has been destroyed in an area, through fire or human overuse — plants normally give the earth some protection from wind. Scientists performed two experiments using equal-sized fields containing the same volume of soil. The soil samples were primarily a mixture of sand and silt but differed in clay percentage: Soil 'Z' was 5% clay and Soil 'W' was 40% clay. Large fans simulated wind, and topsoil deflation was measured in kilograms per hectare (kg/ha) after 10 hours of wind.
Experiment 1: Simulated rainfall via sprinklers, run for 4 or 8 hours on fields of each soil type; two additional fields of each type were left un-watered. Soil samples were taken to determine water content percentage, and topsoil deflation was recorded after wind was applied.
Experiment 2: One field remained uncovered; others were covered with different percentages of compost and straw approximating natural vegetative cover. Topsoil deflation was recorded for each field.

passages.title: Petroleum Systems
passages.body_text:
The origin of petroleum begins with the formation of organic matter, burial of that organic matter in a basin, and maturation of the organic content under pressure and temperature at burial depths. A petroleum system includes source rocks, reservoir rocks, traps, migration paths, and seals. Hydrocarbons that mature in source rocks migrate into reservoirs — sedimentary rocks (clastic or carbonate) with sufficient interconnected pore space.
Migration of matured hydrocarbons proceeds in separate phases, from higher to lower potential and from deepest to shallowest. Hydrocarbons migrate into different types of traps — anticlinal, fault, and salt-related stratigraphic traps. Reservoir seals are low-permeability rocks that drape hydrocarbon traps, ensuring entrapped fluids do not escape. Integration of geology, geophysics, and petrophysics is key to predicting reservoir geometry and volume in reserve assessment.

passages.title: Earth's Magnetic Field: Two Scientific Viewpoints
passages.body_text:
Earth's magnetic field is defined by North and South Poles that align generally with the axis of rotation. Lines of magnetic force flow into Earth in the northern hemisphere and out in the southern hemisphere. At the poles, the force is vertical; at the equator, it is horizontal; in between, it is at an intermediate angle.
Scientist 1: The field is attributed to a dynamo effect of circulating electric current in the molten outer core. Electric currents cause magnetic fields, so circulating currents in the molten metallic core are the field's origin. When conducting fluid flows across an existing magnetic field, induced currents create another magnetic field that, when reinforcing, sustains a self-sustaining dynamo. The outer core, sitting atop the hot iron inner core, churns and moves, with cyclones powered by the Coriolis effect of Earth's rotation. These complex, unpredictable motions generate the fluctuating field, evidenced by constant changes and reversals in polarity. Notably, iron above its Curie temperature (1043 K) loses its magnetic properties — so the field is caused not by magnetized iron deposits, but by electric currents in the liquid outer core.
Scientist 2: The field is similar to a bar magnet tilted 11 degrees from Earth's spin axis, created by coordinated motion of electrons within iron atoms. The core consists of metals; the solid iron inner core (70% as wide as the Moon) would exhibit ferromagnetism, the natural magnetic tendency of iron. The core has its own rotation and is surrounded by a "sea" of molten rock. The field grows and wanes, and the poles drift and occasionally flip as the inner core's rotation changes. Daily fluctuations largely result from interference by solar wind.

passages.title: Bone Remodeling, Osteoporosis, and Osteopetrosis
passages.body_text:
Despite their hard, persistent nature and relatively static proportions, human bones are an extraordinarily dynamic tissue that is continuously resorbed, remodeled, and renewed. Maintaining these processes requires precisely regulated homeostatic mechanisms to preserve adequate bone strength, structure, and density.
Bone resorption is triggered by parathyroid hormone (PTH) under conditions of low calcium. PTH binds to receptors on osteoblasts, which upregulate the signaling protein RANKL. RANKL binds to the receptor RANK on osteoclast precursors, activating the transcription factor NF-κB, signaling them to differentiate into functioning osteoclasts. OPG, produced by osteoblasts, competitively blocks RANKL, preventing this signaling. Net bone formation or resorption can be described as a function of the ratio of OPG to RANKL. Osteoblasts synthesize and arrange bone matrix proteins, chiefly depositing collagen to form new bone.
Osteoporosis is a disease characterized by decreased bone density and increasingly porous bone structure. It affects over half of the U.S. population over 50 and is overwhelmingly more common among postmenopausal women, largely due to the marked decrease in estrogen levels, since estrogen plays an important role in regulating RANKL and OPG.
Autosomal recessive osteopetrosis (ARO), or "marble bone disease," is characterized by excessively thick, dense, yet brittle bones. ARO is congenital, affecting individuals from birth due to genetic anomalies, typically resulting in death by age ten. One variant results from a mutation in the gene coding for RANKL; others from defects in OPG. A hypothetical study hopes to determine the epidemiology of osteoporosis and ARO in the United States by attaching a survey to annual political election ballots over ten years, with a yearly sample size of nearly 10 million, asking simple yes/no questions about whether the voter has ever had either condition.

passages.title: Glycolysis, Na+/K+ Homeostasis, and Septic Shock
passages.body_text:
The myocellular transmembrane Na+ gradient is important for proper cellular function. During septic shock, disruption of Na+ homeostasis often occurs, leading to decreased membrane potential and increased intracellular Na+. Failure of cellular energy metabolism is a common symptom in septic patients who do not respond to therapeutics. Because normal intracellular Na+ levels are maintained by the Na+/K+ ATPase, it is important to understand how metabolic energy production is linked to cation transport.
Experiments evaluated the effects of glycolytic inhibition on cellular Na+ and K+ concentrations and lactate production in rat skeletal myocytes. Muscle fibers were extracted and incubated in normal media (control), glucose-free media (G(-)), and glucose-free media with various concentrations of the glycolytic inhibitor iodoacetate (IAA), which directly prevents the formation of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate. After one hour, tissues were assayed for intracellular Na+ and K+ content and lactate production. Cellular viability was determined by measuring released lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), an indicator of cell death.
Researchers also examined the effect of disrupting oxidative phosphorylation, using carbonyl-cyanide m-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP), an ionophore that allows protons to move freely through membranes. No correlation between Na+/K+ content and oxidative phosphorylation was found.

passages.title: Bacterial Temperature Classifications
passages.body_text:
Bacteria can be categorized by how they respond, in terms of reproduction and growth, to certain temperatures: psychrophiles, psychrotrophs, mesophiles, and thermophiles. Minimal growth temperature is the lowest point at which bacteria will reproduce; optimum growth point is the temperature at which they reproduce most efficiently; maximum growth point is the highest temperature at which they will still respond, beyond which they will not reproduce at all.
Table 1 — Classifications:
Psychrophile: Minimum below 0°C | Optimum 10-15°C | Maximum below 20°C
Psychrotroph: Minimum 0-5°C | Optimum 15°C | Maximum 30°C
Mesophile: Minimum 5-25°C | Optimum 18-45°C | Maximum 30-50°C
Thermophile: Minimum 25-45°C | Optimum 50-60°C | Maximum 60-90°C
(Table 2, referenced in the questions, lists specific bacterial species with their measured minimum/optimum/maximum growth temperatures, including Listeria monocytogenes [minimum ~1°C, maximum ~45°C], Escherichia coli [optimum ~37°C], Micrococcus cryophilus [range ~0-30°C], and others.)

passages.title: The Dense Membrane: Two Biologists' Hypotheses
passages.body_text:
Where do extracellular biological materials come from? Many substances accumulate outside cells (extracellular), including bone, teeth, cartilage, ligaments, and membranes. One particular membrane appears in a space between two layers of cells; it is known as the dense membrane, and the cell layers are known as the outer cell layer and the inner cell layer. The cells of the two layers are suspected of producing the dense membrane.
Biologist 1: When the dense membrane is fully formed, it is possible to scrape off large numbers of cells from the outer layer, grind them up, and subject them to chemical tests. Biologist 1 found these cells contain many of the same biochemicals found in the dense membrane, and concluded the dense membrane is therefore formed only by the cells of the outer layer.
Biologist 2: Using a powerful microscope, Biologist 2 saw what appeared to be small particles of the dense membrane within individual cells of the inner layer. These cells deposited the particles in the space between the inner and outer layers as the dense membrane was forming. Chemical tests showed these particles were composed of the same biochemicals as the dense membrane. Biologist 2 concluded the dense membrane was produced only by the inner layer of cells.

passages.body_text: Figure 1 shows the relative absorption of light by chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b versus wavelength of light, from 400 nm to 750 nm. Figure 2 shows the average rate of photosynthesis at various wavelengths, as a percent of the average rate of photosynthesis at 670 nm.

passages.title: Gastrulation in Vertebrate Embryos
passages.body_text:
Gastrulation is one of the most dramatic and crucial stages of vertebrate embryogenesis. The embryo, at first simply a hollow ball of cells, is transformed into a multilayered structure with a central gut tube and bilateral symmetry. The outer layer formed during gastrulation becomes the ectoderm, the middle layer the mesoderm, and the inner layer the endoderm. Since interactions between these three layers determine the embryo's further developmental fate, gastrulation events are vital for proper organism development.
Gastrulation begins when cells around the embryonic blastopore begin to invaginate, moving toward the inside of the embryo. The site where invagination initiates is the dorsal lip of the blastopore, which acts as an organizer — inducing the tissue directly around it to begin invagination, while triggering tissue further away to adopt other specific cell fates. Cells of the dorsal lip were later found to secrete a diffusible signalling substance that slowly degrades after secretion. Cells at different distances from the dorsal lip are exposed to different concentrations of the substance, leading to different signalled behaviors. Due to its effect on morphogenesis, this substance is called a morphogen.

passages.title: Bacteriophage Lambda: Lytic vs. Lysogenic Pathways
passages.body_text:
Bacteriophage lambda is a non-enveloped DNA virus whose host is the bacterium E. coli. Infection begins when the virus adsorbs to the host cell surface. Once attached, the phage injects its DNA across the plasma membrane into the cytoplasm, where it is transformed from a linear strand to a circular one. After this point, infection may take one of two pathways:
Lytic Pathway: After injection, the circularized DNA is transcribed and translated by the host cell's machinery; the resulting proteins make up the future viral capsid. The lambda DNA undergoes several rounds of replication, then is packaged into new capsids. Multiple new viral particles form, ultimately causing lysis (bursting) of the host cell, releasing the new lambda phages.
Lysogenic Pathway: After injection, the circularized DNA directs production of a viral protein called integrase, which causes the circular lambda DNA to integrate into the bacterial chromosome. Once inserted, the lambda DNA (now a provirus) is replicated along with the E. coli host cell, remaining hidden and inactive for multiple replications. If the E. coli host is damaged by UV light or ionizing radiation, the latent lambda provirus can excise itself from the chromosome and enter the lytic pathway.

passages.title: Staph Mutation and Antibiotic Resistance Experiments
passages.body_text:
A set of experiments was carried out to isolate unusual mutants in the bacterium Staph. Normal Staph cells grow well on a minimal nutrient medium of agar plus a solution of glucose, salts, and ammonia. Staph can also grow on a medium with more complex sugars like lactose, since they normally have enzymes to convert complex sugars to glucose.
Experiment 1: A sample of normal Staph was treated with X-rays to produce genetic mutations, then spread across a dish of minimal nutrient medium containing the antibiotic ampicillin, which kills normal Staph. After overnight incubation, no bacterial colonies were found growing.
Experiment 2: The experiment was repeated exactly, using the same original sample. This time, after incubation, two colonies (Colony A and Colony B) were found growing on the medium.
Experiment 3: Samples from Colony A and Colony B were spread across two different ampicillin-containing media — Medium X (the typical minimal glucose medium) and Medium Y (identical, but with lactose instead of glucose as the only nutrient sugar). After incubation: Colony A grew on both X and Y. Colony B grew on X but showed no growth on Y.

passages.title: Fish Biodiversity and the Nile Perch
passages.body_text:
Fishes are appropriate indicators of trends in aquatic biodiversity because their enormous variety reflects a wide range of environmental conditions. Fish also have a major impact on the distribution and abundance of other organisms in the waters they inhabit. The proximate causes of fish species decline can be divided into five broad categories: (1) competition for food, (2) habitat alteration, (3) pollution, (4) introduction of exotic species, and (5) commercial exploitation.
For example, since the building of the High Dam in Aswan, a lot of changes happened to biodiversity in south Egypt: the region's fishing industries struggled to grow because the fish that lived in the river and lakes were predominantly small-bodied and bony. To solve this for commercial use, the Nile perch was introduced. The Nile perch can grow far larger than many other Nile fish and was well suited for commercial fishing. Being carnivorous, the Nile perch preyed on the smaller native fish, and as its population grew, populations of the other species plummeted.

passages.title: Mineral Hardness and the Mohs Scale
passages.body_text:
Geologists have identified more than two thousand minerals and use many properties to identify them — streak, color, luster, transparency, hardness, cleavage, crystal system, density, and fracture.
German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs (1773-1839) devised the Mohs scale of mineral hardness in 1812, selecting ten minerals (talc, gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase, quartz, topaz, corundum, and diamond) because they were common or readily available. The scale is not linear, but somewhat arbitrary — equal steps on the Mohs scale do not represent equal increases in absolute hardness.

passages.title: Earthquake Seismic Wave Propagation Model
passages.body_text:
Earthquakes disrupt the infrastructure of buildings and dwellings by displacing the ground beneath them through surface waves. The epicenter is the point on Earth's surface vertically above the focus. Surface waves propagate from the epicenter outward and are directly affected by the density of the ground through which they propagate. Wave strength is characterized as strong, moderate, or weak.
A seismologist assembled a circular small-scale model with varying ground densities to study the effect of ground density on wave propagation. Ground density and propagation duration were controlled. In each study, earth and clay were laid down in a circular pattern with increasing density, and a large speaker was placed 2 m below the surface at the epicenter to mimic an earthquake.
Study 1: 60 dB.
Study 2: 80 dB — resulting waveform: Strong waves extend to ~2 m, Moderate waves extend to ~4 m, Weak waves extend past 5 m.
Study 3: 100 dB — resulting waveform: Strong waves extend past 3.5 m, Moderate waves extend past 5 m.

passages.title: Pangaea, Continental Drift, and Fossils
passages.body_text:
About 300 million years ago, Earth had one massive supercontinent called Pangaea, surrounded by a single ocean called Panthalassa. Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist who introduced his theory of continental drift in 1922, claimed that Pangaea began splitting apart by the Mesozoic era (around 220 million years ago) into pieces that achieved their present positions as modern continents during the late Cenozoic era.
The explanation for Pangaea's formation ushered in the modern theory of plate tectonics, which posits that Earth's outer shell is broken into several plates that slide over the mantle. Over the planet's 3.5-billion-year history, several supercontinents have formed and broken apart as a result of churning and circulation in Earth's mantle.

passages.title: Io's Volcanic Activity: Two Scientific Viewpoints
passages.body_text:
As Voyager 2 approached Jupiter in 1979, images of its moon Io revealed what appeared to be an erupting volcano on a celestial body otherwise devoid of an atmosphere or liquid. Additional photos revealed Io to be an incredibly geologically active world with extensive sulfur deposits on its surface.
Scientist 1: Io is caught in a gravitational "tug of war" between Jupiter and the outer "Galilean" moons, which is the core driver of its extreme volcanic activity. This activity, characterized by extensive flows of molten sulfur, makes Io's volcanism quite different from Earth's, since sulfur melts at a much lower temperature than the lava flows observed on Earth.
Scientist 2: An alternate theory suggests Io's volcanoes are, in fact, similar to those on Earth. Based on the Voyager photos, this scientist argues for the existence of 10 km (6.2 mile) tall volcanic mountains composed primarily of silicate rock — since tall mountains require the structural strength of silicate rocks, these volcanoes must be similar in composition to those on Earth.

passages.title: Rare Earth Elements in Igneous and Sedimentary Rocks
passages.body_text:
Rock types can often be differentiated by the rare earth elements (REEs) they contain. Table 1 shows the average concentration of two REEs, neodymium and samarium, in four igneous rock types (oceanic basalt, continental basalt, andesite, granite) and three sedimentary rock types (shale, sandstone, dolomite).
Figure 1 shows the relative concentration of REEs in various igneous rock types and in sedimentary rocks (taken as a group), where relative concentration = average REE concentration in the rock type ÷ average REE concentration in meteorites.

passages.title: Urease and Nitrogen Metabolism in Soybeans
passages.body_text:
Urease is an enzyme used by plants to break down urea (a nitrogen-containing compound) into carbon dioxide and ammonia. Plants need nitrogen to grow and can obtain it from ammonia, but not from urea. In soybean plants, there are two different kinds of urease — one produced in the seeds and one produced in the leaves. Mutations in the soybean's chromosomes can stop production of either enzyme. In the following experiments, three types of soybean plants were used: normal soybeans, and two mutant strains — Strain 1 (lacking seed urease) and Strain 2 (lacking leaf urease).
Experiment 1: Separate areas in a field were planted with normal, Strain 1, and Strain 2 soybeans. All types grew, flowered, and produced seeds equally well, with no externally detectable differences among the strains.
Experiment 2: Small pieces of plant tissue of equal weight were obtained from each type of soybean plant and placed on media in culture dishes — half on media containing urea, half on media containing ammonia, as a controlled nitrogen source. After 30 days, weight gain for each callus sample was determined: Normal gained weight on both; Strain 1 gained weight on both; Strain 2 gained weight on ammonia, but poorly on urea.

passages.title: The Protein Hypothesis vs. the DNA Hypothesis
passages.body_text:
In the 1940s, scientists thought all genetic material was contained in structures called chromosomes, found only in the nucleus of a cell (not in the cytoplasm). Chromosomes are composed of two types of molecules: proteins and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). Two scientists in the 1940s debated whether genes are made of proteins or DNA.
Protein Hypothesis: Genes are made only of proteins. Cells contain 20 different amino acids that can be arranged in a virtually infinite number of ways to make different proteins; the number and arrangement of amino acids within a protein form the codes that carry hereditary information. In contrast, only 4 different nucleotides make up DNA, believed to form chains only in certain ratios — so the number of different combinations DNA can carry is much smaller than what proteins can carry.
DNA Hypothesis: Genes are made only of DNA. DNA is found exclusively in the cell's nucleus, whereas proteins are found throughout the nucleus and cytoplasm. Additionally, the amount of protein in a cell varies from cell type to cell type, even within the same animal. Though DNA is less abundant than protein, the amount of DNA is consistent from cell type to cell type within the same animal, except for gametes (reproductive cells), which have half the amount of DNA — and half the typical number of chromosomes — as other cells in the body. Thus, the amount of DNA in a cell is correlated with the number of chromosomes in the cell; no such correlation is found for proteins.
